title: Self-Healing Diffusion Monte Carlo applied to a simple fermionic model: A critical assessment of the method
authors: Michel Caffarel, Manon Pinar, Anthony Scemama
abstract: We investigate the Self-Healing Diffusion Monte Carlo (SHDMC) method using a one-dimensional model with periodic boundary conditions. An inversion symmetry is introduced to mimic the antisymmetry property of fermionic wavefunctions, with the bosonic and fermionic sectors being modeled by the even and odd eigenstates, respectively. As in realistic fermionic systems, the nodal structure is only partially constrained by symmetry, making this model a non-trivial testbed for nodal optimization algorithms such as SHDMC. We show that the nodal evolution under SHDMC iterations can be cast into a dynamical system exhibiting both attractive and repulsive fixed points. In the standard formulation of SHDMC applied to this model, the fixed-node energy is found to increase upon iteration, and the node converges to a wrong value, indicating that SHDMC does not always converge to the correct solution. We further show that this problem is partially cured by modifying the nodal update criterion to give more importance to the nodal region. Achieving convergence in the general case very likely requires the use of a localized basis set, as is the case for this model.
summary: This work provides a critical assessment of the Self-Healing Diffusion Monte Carlo (SHDMC) method when applied to fermionic systems. The authors demonstrate that the standard implementation fails to converge to the correct fixed-node energy due to systematic node deterioration. They propose and validate modifications, such as emphasizing the nodal region or using localized basis sets, which are necessary for achieving accurate results.
main_problem: The paper critically assesses the Self-Healing Diffusion Monte Carlo (SHDMC) method for improving the nodal surface of fermionic wavefunctions.
main_result: Standard SHDMC fails for the tested fermionic model, causing the fixed-node energy to increase monotonically; however, modifying the nodal update criterion or using localized basis sets can partially restore convergence.
method: The authors employ an iterative fixed-node calculation within the SHDMC framework, comparing standard criteria against modified local criteria and localized basis sets.
model_or_system: The study uses a one-dimensional model with periodic boundary conditions, incorporating an inversion symmetry to mimic the nodal structure of fermionic wavefunctions.
key_observables: Fixed-node energy ($E_{FN}$), nodal convergence (node position $	heta_N$), and the stability index ($\eta$).
important_parameters: The degree of nodal constraint ($\epsilon$) and the choice of basis set (Fourier vs. localized).
main_assumptions: The primary assumption is that the nodal structure can be iteratively optimized using the SHDMC procedure, which is shown to be conditionally true.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the monotonic increase of $E_{FN}$ under standard SHDMC, and show that modified criteria or localized bases allow the node position to converge toward the correct physical value.
paper_structure: The paper progresses by first establishing the failure of standard SHDMC, then proposing and testing a modification focusing on the nodal region, and finally demonstrating improved convergence using localized basis sets.
why_interesting: The rigorous analysis of convergence failure and the proposal of specific algorithmic fixes (like local basis sets) are highly relevant to developing robust numerical techniques for strongly correlated quantum systems.

Figure 1 displays the fixed-node energy as a function of the nodal position θFN; the exact energy is indicated by the horizontal line. As expected from the variational principle[12], the fixed-node energy is above the exact energy and reaches its minimum when the angle equals the exact value. This exact angle, denoted as θex, is in full agreement with the node obtained independently from the exact wave function computed in the ϕk Fourier basis set. We stress again that this node (and its image under inversion) cannot be inferred from symmetry alone: as in realistic fermionic systems, it depends on the specific form of the potential and requires solving the Schr¨odinger equation.
